assessmentSummary.identity: A grounded dynamic compression exercise. The athlete remains seated and lifts one or both legs through an owned pike or straddle range without suspending bodyweight through the hands. Knee angle, unilateral versus bilateral execution, pike versus straddle, hand position, lift height, tempo, and dose are controlled variant or modifier dimensions.
currentCardFindings: The historical Straddle Compression Lift is a valid variant but too narrow to represent the full grounded dynamic compression identity.
Pike and straddle change hip-abduction range and flexibility interaction while preserving the same seated dynamic hip-flexion action.
Bent-knee, unilateral, and bilateral versions materially change lever, symmetry, coordination, and difficulty and should be explicit variants.
Hand position, stable blocks or handles, lift height, pause, tempo, range, and set volume are delivery modifiers when the seated dynamic action remains unchanged.
L-sit, V-sit, Manna, hanging leg raise, and press-to-handstand work change support action or principal movement intent and remain separate identities.
The former 40/20/40 baseline materially understated bilateral long-lever hip-flexion, knee-extension, trunk, straddle-symmetry, and controlled-lowering demand.
Exercise difficulty is assessed only as exercise complexity and physical difficulty, with overall equal to their maximum. This exercise card carries no athlete or class proficiency level.
The legacy canonical slug remains stable for compatibility; canonical name and aliases now expose the broader Seated Compression Lift identity.
All five media links remain candidate-only. Metadata health is not exact-match, safety, accessibility, or content approval.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: Knee flexion shortens the lever while retaining a seated bilateral lift, trunk control, breathing, and controlled lowering.
One straight leg lengthens the lever but reduces simultaneous bilateral demand and adds side-to-side control and symmetric exposure.
Both extended legs increase bilateral lever, knee-extension, hip-flexion, trunk, and controlled-lowering demand.
Straddle preserves the dynamic lift but adds hip-abduction range, adductor control, bilateral symmetry, and additional frontal-plane organization.

proposedLoadProfile.recoveryHours: Count the work with other high-volume hip-flexion, compression, hanging-leg-raise, L-sit, V-sit, press, and aggressive active-flexibility training. Short submaximal sets may recover quickly; long-lever, high-range, high-volume, or near-failure work may need more time.

proposedDeliveryProfiles.dose: Two to four sets of four to eight controlled reps for long-lever variants or six to twelve for bent-knee, with 45 to 90 seconds rest and at least two clean reps in reserve.
proposedDeliveryProfiles.qualityGate: Declared lever and position remain unchanged; the trunk does not rock; legs clear and lower quietly through owned range; breathing continues.

athlete: Sit in the selected pike or straddle.
Place the hands where prescribed without pulling.
Lift from the hips without rocking.
Pause only if declared, then lower quietly.
Stop before the lever, range, or breathing changes.
coach: Select knee angle, laterality, pike or straddle, hand position, range, tempo, and dose before the set.
Observe front and side for trunk rock, knee position, symmetry, lift height, and controlled lowering.
Regress lever or range rather than accepting momentum.
Stop and substitute for pain, pinching, neurologic symptoms, or uncontrolled cramping.

proposedProgramming.sequence: Use after general and positional preparation but before high-volume hip-flexion, hanging, L-sit, V-sit, or press work.

athleteQuestions: Could you lift and lower without rocking?
Did the selected pike or straddle feel like active effort rather than a pinch?
Could the next rep match the first?
coachQuestions: Did lever, range, symmetry, trunk position, lowering, or symptoms limit the set first?
Was a variant or modifier changed and recorded?
Does the next exercise share hip-flexor or compression fatigue?

claims: The professional progression distinguishes compression-building lead-up work from supported L-sit, V-sit, and Manna positions.
Classify seated dynamic leg lifting as a grounded compression exercise; pike, straddle, knee angle, laterality, hand position, range, and tempo do not by themselves create a new movement identity.
Parallette progressions manipulate knee angle, unilateral versus bilateral legs, straddle, height, and compression demand.
Represent knee angle, laterality, and pike or straddle as controlled variants; represent hand position, support height, range, pause, tempo, and volume as modifiers.
Training exercises involving hip flexion recruit hip-flexor musculature and can also require abdominal activation.
For a seated leg lift, describe active hip flexion as primary and trunk/pelvic control and knee extension as important contributors without claiming isolated-muscle training.
Shortening the knee lever and moving from one leg to two legs changes the mechanical demand of compression work.
Pike versus straddle changes frontal-plane hip position and available range, while trunk rocking or hand pulling changes execution rather than successful completion.
Exercise prescription should account for technique, load, fatigue, and progression instead of relying on a generic label.
Candidate difficulty rises with longer bilateral lever, higher owned range, less compensation, and added straddle symmetry; overall is derived only from exercise complexity and physical difficulty.
Hip-flexion exercises can impose meaningful local hip-flexor and abdominal demand even without external load.
Track compression alongside other high-volume hip-flexion, hanging-leg-raise, L-sit, V-sit, and press work; stop before rocking, knee change, range loss, or uncontrolled lowering.
Safe resistance training requires suitable space, equipment, instruction, progression, and individualized readiness.
Require a non-slip surface, clear leg arc, owned seated range, pain-free execution, controlled lowering, and a declared lever and position.
Training variables should be selected to preserve technique and match the intended adaptation.
Use short controlled sets with a visible repetition reserve, sufficient rest, and a cap that prevents active-compression practice from becoming momentum-based conditioning.
Compression progressions emphasize actively lifting the legs and manipulating knee angle and leg position.
Cue a declared seated position, active lift from the hips, stable trunk, unchanged knee angle, controlled lower, breathing, and an early stop.
Exercise order, training volume, rest, and progression should reflect the session goal and cumulative demand.
Place precise compression work before competing hip-flexor and trunk fatigue; count it with L-sit, V-sit, hanging-leg-raise, press, and active-flexibility volume.
Individual development should be based on readiness and movement competence.
Give the athlete plain-language self-checks for trunk rocking, knee position, range, quiet lowering, symptoms, breathing, and whether the next repetition can match the first.
Qualified supervision and technique-focused progression are central to safe resistance exercise.
The coach should preselect lever, position, range, tempo, and dose; observe from front and side; and regress before compensations replace the intended action.
Knee angle, one-leg work, bilateral work, straddle, and compression range form a progression family, while supported L-sit, V-sit, and Manna impose different support identities.

Use explicit variants for meaningful lever or leg-position changes, modifier annotations for range, hand position, tempo, and dose, and separate definitions when bodyweight support or a different principal action appears.
